Since \(4! = 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24\), the sentence is correct.

Let \(p:\) India is a country (T) and \(q:\) Himalayas is a river (F). The Himalayas is a mountain range, not a river, so \(q\) is F.

The conjunction \(p \wedge q\) is \(T \wedge F = F\).

The identity \(\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = \cos 2\theta\) holds for all \(\theta \in R\).

It is a **statement** in logic (an open conditional that is decidable over whole numbers).

For \(x\) a whole number, \(x + 6 = 0\) would give \(x = -6\), which is not a whole number. So no whole number satisfies \(x + 6 = 0\); the implication 'if \(x\) is a whole number then \(x + 6 = 0\)' is false (take \(x = 0\): antecedent T, consequent F).

**Truth value: F (False).**

Let \(p:\) \(\sqrt{5}\) is irrational, and \(q:\) \(3\sqrt{5}\) is a complex number. The statement is \(p \wedge q\).

\(\sqrt{5}\) is irrational, so \(p\) is T. But \(3\sqrt{5}\) is a real (irrational) number, not a (non-real) complex number as intended, so \(q\) is F.

Hence \(p \wedge q \equiv T \wedge F = F\).

**Truth value: F (False).**

The statement is \(\forall n \in N\), (\(n^2 + n\) is even) \(\wedge\) (\(n^2 - n\) is odd).

Now \(n^2 + n = n(n+1)\) is a product of two consecutive integers, hence always even (T). But \(n^2 - n = n(n-1)\) is also a product of two consecutive integers, hence always **even**, not odd. So the second part is F.

A conjunction with a false part is false.

**Truth value: F (False).**

The statement is \(\exists n \in N\) such that \(n + 5 > 10\), i.e. \(n > 5\).

For example \(n = 6 \in N\) gives \(6 + 5 = 11 > 10\). Such an \(n\) exists.

**Truth value: T (True).**

Let \(p:\) the square of any even number is odd, and \(q:\) the cube of any odd number is odd. The statement is \(p \vee q\).

The square of an even number is even, so \(p\) is F. The cube of an odd number is odd (e.g. \(3^3 = 27\)); in general odd \(\times\) odd \(\times\) odd is odd, so \(q\) is T.

Hence \(p \vee q \equiv F \vee T = T\).

The statement is a conditional: in \(\triangle ABC\), if all sides are equal then all angles are equal.

An equilateral triangle (all sides equal) is equiangular (each angle \(60^\circ\)), so the implication holds.

This fails for \(n = 1\): \(1 + 6 = 7 \not> 8\) (also fails for \(n = 2\)). So it is not true for all \(n\).

Since \(7 \in A\) and \(7 + 8 = 15\), such an \(x\) exists.

This fails for \(x = 7\): \(7 + 5 = 12 \not< 12\) (also fails for \(x = 8, 9\)). So it does not hold for all \(x\).

For example \(x = 4 \in A\) gives \(4 + 7 = 11 \geq 11\). Such an \(x\) exists.

**Truth value: T (True).**

The largest value is at \(x = 9\): \(3 \times 9 = 27 \not\leq 25\). So it fails for \(x = 9\) (and \(x = 8: 24 \leq 25\) holds, but one failure is enough).

Using \(\sim(\forall x, P(x)) \equiv \exists x, \sim P(x)\), the negation is:

\(\exists n \in A\) such that \(n + 7 \leq 6\).

**In words:** There exists \(n \in A\) such that \(n + 7\) is not greater than \(6\).

The given statement is \(\exists x \in A\) such that \(x + 9 \leq 15\).

Using \(\sim(\exists x, P(x)) \equiv \forall x, \sim P(x)\), the negation is:

\(\forall x \in A\), \(x + 9 > 15\).

**In words:** For every \(x \in A\), \(x + 9\) is greater than \(15\).

The statement 'Some triangles are equilateral triangle' is an existential statement (\(\exists\)).

Using \(\sim(\exists x, P(x)) \equiv \forall x, \sim P(x)\), its negation is:

**No triangle is an equilateral triangle.**

(Equivalently: All triangles are non-equilateral triangles.)

Truth table for \(p \to (q \to p)\):

| \(p\) | \(q\) | \(q \to p\) | \(p \to (q \to p)\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T |
| T | F | T | T |
| F | T | F | T |
| F | F | T | T |

The last column is T in every row, so \(p \to (q \to p)\) is a **tautology**.

Truth table for \((\sim p \vee \sim q) \leftrightarrow [\sim(p \wedge q)]\):

| \(p\) | \(q\) | \(\sim p\) | \(\sim q\) | \(\sim p \vee \sim q\) | \(p \wedge q\) | \(\sim(p \wedge q)\) | \((\sim p \vee \sim q) \leftrightarrow \sim(p \wedge q)\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | F | F | T | F | T |
| T | F | F | T | T | F | T | T |
| F | T | T | F | T | F | T | T |
| F | F | T | T | T | F | T | T |

The last column is T in every row, so the pattern is a **tautology** (this is one of De Morgan's laws).

Truth table for \(\sim(\sim p \wedge \sim q) \vee q\):

| \(p\) | \(q\) | \(\sim p\) | \(\sim q\) | \(\sim p \wedge \sim q\) | \(\sim(\sim p \wedge \sim q)\) | \(\sim(\sim p \wedge \sim q) \vee q\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | F | F | T | T |
| T | F | F | T | F | T | T |
| F | T | T | F | F | T | T |
| F | F | T | T | T | F | F |

The final column is \(T, T, T, F\), so the pattern is a **contingency** (note \(\sim(\sim p \wedge \sim q) \equiv p \vee q\), and \((p \vee q) \vee q \equiv p \vee q\)).

Let \(t \equiv p \wedge q\). Truth table for \([(p \wedge q) \vee r] \wedge [\sim r \vee (p \wedge q)]\):

| \(p\) | \(q\) | \(r\) | \(p \wedge q\) | \((p\wedge q)\vee r\) | \(\sim r\) | \(\sim r \vee (p\wedge q)\) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | T | F | T | T |
| T | T | F | T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | T | F | T | F | F | F |
| T | F | F | F | F | T | T | F |
| F | T | T | F | T | F | F | F |
| F | T | F | F | F | T | T | F |
| F | F | T | F | T | F | F | F |
| F | F | F | F | F | T | T | F |

The final column contains both T and F, so the pattern is a **contingency**. (It is in fact equivalent to \(p \wedge q\).)

| \(p\) | \(q\) | \(r\) | \(\sim p \vee q\) | \(q \to r\) | \(A=(\sim p\vee q)\wedge(q\to r)\) | \(p \to r\) | \(A \to (p\to r)\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| T | F | F | F | T | F | F | T |

The last column is T in every row, so the pattern is a **tautology**.

| \(p\) | \(q\) | \(p \to q\) | \(\sim q\) | \((p\to q)\wedge \sim q\) | \(\sim p\) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | F | F | F | T |
| T | F | F | T | F | F | T |
| F | T | T | F | F | T | T |
| F | F | T | T | T | T | T |

The last column is T in every row, so the pattern is a **tautology** (this is the valid form modus tollens).

Truth table for \([(p \vee q) \wedge \sim p] \wedge \sim q\):

| \(p\) | \(q\) | \(p \vee q\) | \(\sim p\) | \((p\vee q)\wedge \sim p\) | \(\sim q\) | Result |

| T | F | T | F | F | T | F |
| F | T | T | T | T | F | F |

The last column is F in every row, so the pattern is a **contradiction**.

| \(p\) | \(q\) | \(p \to q\) | \(\sim q\) | \(p \wedge \sim q\) | Result |

\(p \wedge q\) is T only when **both** \(p\) and \(q\) are T. With \(p = T, q = T\), we also get \(p \vee q = T\), which is consistent.

**Answer: \(p = T\) and \(q = T\).**

Given \((p \vee q)\) is T and \((p \vee q) \to q\) is F.

An implication \(X \to q\) is F only when \(X\) is T and \(q\) is F. Here \(X = p \vee q\) is T (given) and \(q\) is F.

Since \(p \vee q = T\) with \(q = F\), we must have \(p = T\).

**Answer: \(p = T\) and \(q = F\).**

Given \((p \wedge q)\) is F and \((p \wedge q) \to q\) is T.

Here \(p \wedge q\) is F, so the antecedent of the implication is F; then \((p \wedge q) \to q\) is automatically T for any truth value of \(q\). Thus the second condition gives no extra restriction.

The only condition is \(p \wedge q = F\), which holds whenever at least one of \(p, q\) is F.

**Answer:** \(p\) and \(q\) cannot both be determined uniquely. Any of \((p,q) = (T,F), (F,T), (F,F)\) satisfies the conditions; i.e. **at least one of \(p, q\) is F.**

Prove \(p \leftrightarrow q \equiv \sim(p \wedge \sim q) \wedge \sim(q \wedge \sim p)\) using rules of logic.

Start from the right-hand side and apply De Morgan's law and conditional laws:

\(\sim(p \wedge \sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee q \equiv p \to q\).

\(\sim(q \wedge \sim p) \equiv \sim q \vee p \equiv q \to p\).

Therefore

\(\sim(p \wedge \sim q) \wedge \sim(q \wedge \sim p) \equiv (p \to q) \wedge (q \to p)\).

By the definition of the biconditional, \((p \to q) \wedge (q \to p) \equiv p \leftrightarrow q\).

Hence \(p \leftrightarrow q \equiv \sim(p \wedge \sim q) \wedge \sim(q \wedge \sim p)\). **Proved.**

Prove \(\sim p \wedge q \equiv (p \vee q) \wedge \sim p\) using rules of logic.

Start from the right-hand side and apply the distributive law:

\((p \vee q) \wedge \sim p \equiv (p \wedge \sim p) \vee (q \wedge \sim p)\).

Since \(p \wedge \sim p \equiv F\) (complement law):

\(\equiv F \vee (q \wedge \sim p) \equiv q \wedge \sim p\) (identity law).

By commutativity, \(q \wedge \sim p \equiv \sim p \wedge q\).

Hence \(\sim p \wedge q \equiv (p \vee q) \wedge \sim p\). **Proved.**

Prove \(\sim(p \vee q) \vee (\sim p \wedge q) \equiv \sim p\) using rules of logic.

By De Morgan's law, \(\sim(p \vee q) \equiv \sim p \wedge \sim q\). So the left-hand side becomes

\((\sim p \wedge \sim q) \vee (\sim p \wedge q)\).

Apply the distributive law (take \(\sim p\) common):

\(\equiv \sim p \wedge (\sim q \vee q)\).

Since \(\sim q \vee q \equiv T\) (complement law):

\(\equiv \sim p \wedge T \equiv \sim p\) (identity law).

Hence \(\sim(p \vee q) \vee (\sim p \wedge q) \equiv \sim p\). **Proved.**

Negate \((p \vee q) \wedge (q \vee \sim r)\).

Using De Morgan's law \(\sim(A \wedge B) \equiv \sim A \vee \sim B\):

\(\sim[(p \vee q) \wedge (q \vee \sim r)] \equiv \sim(p \vee q) \vee \sim(q \vee \sim r)\).

Apply De Morgan's law to each bracket (and \(\sim(\sim r) \equiv r\)):

\(\equiv (\sim p \wedge \sim q) \vee (\sim q \wedge r)\).

**Negation: \((\sim p \wedge \sim q) \vee (\sim q \wedge r)\).**

Negate \(p \wedge (q \vee r)\).

Using De Morgan's law \(\sim(A \wedge B) \equiv \sim A \vee \sim B\):

\(\sim[p \wedge (q \vee r)] \equiv \sim p \vee \sim(q \vee r)\).

Apply De Morgan's law to \(\sim(q \vee r) \equiv \sim q \wedge \sim r\):

\(\equiv \sim p \vee (\sim q \wedge \sim r)\).

**Negation: \(\sim p \vee (\sim q \wedge \sim r)\).**

Negate \((p \to q) \wedge r\).

Using De Morgan's law \(\sim(A \wedge B) \equiv \sim A \vee \sim B\):

\(\sim[(p \to q) \wedge r] \equiv \sim(p \to q) \vee \sim r\).

Using the negation-of-implication rule \(\sim(p \to q) \equiv p \wedge \sim q\):

\(\equiv (p \wedge \sim q) \vee \sim r\).

**Negation: \((p \wedge \sim q) \vee \sim r\).**

Negate \((\sim p \wedge q) \vee (p \wedge \sim q)\).

Using De Morgan's law \(\sim(A \vee B) \equiv \sim A \wedge \sim B\):

\(\sim[(\sim p \wedge q) \vee (p \wedge \sim q)] \equiv \sim(\sim p \wedge q) \wedge \sim(p \wedge \sim q)\).

Apply De Morgan's law to each bracket (and \(\sim(\sim p) \equiv p\), \(\sim(\sim q) \equiv q\)):

\(\equiv (p \vee \sim q) \wedge (\sim p \vee q)\).

**Negation: \((p \vee \sim q) \wedge (\sim p \vee q)\).**

Circuit (i) is \(S_1 \wedge (S_2 \vee S_3)\) and Circuit (ii) is \((S_1 \wedge S_2) \vee (S_1 \wedge S_3)\). Compare by truth table (T = switch closed / current flows):

| \(S_1\) | \(S_2\) | \(S_3\) | \(S_2 \vee S_3\) | \(S_1 \wedge (S_2\vee S_3)\) | \(S_1\wedge S_2\) | \(S_1\wedge S_3\) | \((S_1\wedge S_2)\vee(S_1\wedge S_3)\) |

| T | T | T | T | T | T | T | T |
| T | T | F | T | T | T | F | T |
| T | F | T | T | T | F | T | T |
| T | F | F | F | F | F | F | F |
| F | T | T | T | F | F | F | F |
| F | T | F | T | F | F | F | F |
| F | F | T | T | F | F | F | F |
| F | F | F | F | F | F | F | F |

The two circuit columns (5th and 8th) are identical in every row, so \(S_1 \wedge (S_2 \vee S_3) \equiv (S_1 \wedge S_2) \vee (S_1 \wedge S_3)\).

**Conclusion: the two circuits are logically equivalent** (by the distributive law).
